title: Book 5 — Terpsichore, Chapter 35
paragraphs: So Aristagoras was not able to fulfill his promise to Artaphrenes; and at the same time he was hard pressed by the demand made on him for the expenses of the expedition, and he was afraid both because of the failure of the armament and because he had become an enemy of Megabates; and he supposed he would be stripped of his rule over Miletus. With all these fears, he began to plan revolt. For it happened that just at this time the man who had been marked on the head had come from Histiaeus in Susa, signifying that Aristagoras should revolt from the king. For Histiaeus, wishing to signify to Aristagoras that he should revolt, could find no safe way of doing so—since the roads were guarded—except by shaving the hair of the most trustworthy of his slaves, pricking marks into his head, and then waiting until the hair had grown again. As soon as it had grown, he sent him off to Miletus, giving him no other charge but this: that when he had reached Miletus he should bid Aristagoras shave off his hair and look at his head. The marks, as I have said, signified revolt. Histiaeus did this because he was deeply vexed at being detained at Susa. He had great hopes that if a revolt occurred, he would be let go to the coast; but if no change took place at Miletus, he had no expectation of ever returning there again.
